title: The Grossest Scene in 2026 Gaming Was Designed to Make You Cringe
summary: Most video game gross-out moments involve blood, guts, or monsters. But Mixtape, the new music-driven narrative adventure from Beethoven & Dinosaur, goes for something far more relatable — and somehow even more revolting: a painfully awkward first kiss. Early in the game, protagonist Stacey Rockford reminisces about high school and a mixtape from an old flame named Colin. The memory triggers a flashback where you suddenly take control of both teenagers’ tongues as they fumble through their first makeout session. The game’s art style shifts from its usual stuttery, Spider-Verse-inspired look to something hyper-detailed and grotesque, leaving no slimy detail unrendered. “We were talking about ways of using the medium to feel things that you wouldn't usually feel in a video game, like being grossed out and awkward and embarrassed,” said creative director Johnny Galvatron. “It’s a really teenage experience. The first kiss, and it goes for too long, and it's just foul.” The team spent ages perfecting the ropes of saliva using a particle system, and the result is so effective that even the developers were repulsed. Technical director Roman Maksymshyn had to swap the slurping sounds for bird and nature audio just to get through his workday. “He was like, ‘yeah, I can't hear mouth sounds for another two hours,’” producer Woody Woodward recalled. The scene channels a Ren and Stimpy-style gross-out vibe, zooming in on details that games usually avoid. But Mixtape doesn’t dwell on the ick forever. The game is structured around songs, each with its own unique set piece and mechanics. Once you endure the horrible tongue tango, you never have to repeat it. The rest of the game balances crude humor with genuine coming-of-age storytelling, making the cringe feel purposeful rather than just prankish. So if you can stomach a few minutes of slobbery discomfort, Mixtape offers a refreshingly honest — and hilariously gross — take on teenage memories.
why_it_matters: Mixtape's willingness to dwell on an embarrassing, vulnerable moment shows how video games can stretch beyond power fantasies to explore the messy reality of growing up. By making you literally control the awkwardness, the game challenges the idea that interactive experiences must be cool or heroic. For young teenagers navigating their own social anxieties, this kind of honest portrayal could make games a tool for processing real-life cringe—transforming something normally hidden into a shared, laugh-about-it-later memory.

background_read: Beethoven & Dinosaur is an Australian indie studio known for The Artful Escape (2021), a visually surreal game about a teenage musician searching for his identity through psychedelic worlds.

The 'Spider-Verse' animation style, popularized by the 2018 film Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse, uses comic-book techniques like halftone dots, aggressive motion blur, and a lower frame rate on characters to make them feel drawn rather than perfectly smooth.

Ren and Stimpy (1991–1996) was a controversial cult cartoon famous for extreme close-ups of detailed, ugly anatomy—like warts, oozing, or rotting faces—which made it both influential and notorious in animation history.
The game's format ties each song to a distinct gameplay scenario, similar to a concept album in music, allowing the story to jump between moods, genres, and art styles depending on the soundtrack.

Coming-of-age stories often rely on embarrassing first experiences to create empathy; the awkward first kiss is a nearly universal rite of passage that literature and film have explored for generations, but video games rarely treat it with such cringe-inducing realism.

perspectives.description: Many creators praise the scene for capturing a universal teenage experience that media often idealizes. By refusing to make the first kiss glamorous, Mixtape creates a rare moment of identification; players might actually feel seen, realizing their own awkward memories are normal rather than shameful.

Some critics argue that the exaggerated saliva and close-ups cross a line from relatable to repulsive, potentially making players abandon the game. They worry that the shock value overshadows the story, turning what could be a tender memory into a joke that might discourage young audiences from engaging with the rest of the narrative.

Mixtape follows a tradition of transgressive art—from underground comics to adult cartoons—that uses body horror to provoke emotional reactions. The historical pattern shows that discomfort can be a legitimate storytelling tool, but it often divides audiences, becoming either a cult classic for its boldness or a cautionary tale for excess.

If this approach catches on, future games might deliberately engineer embarrassment, insecurity, or social anxiety as central mechanics, broadening the emotional vocabulary of the medium. Developers could create empathy-building scenarios where failing socially is the point, potentially helping players practice real-life resilience. However, studios will need to carefully balance authenticity with accessibility to avoid alienating those who just want to have fun.
